bp: Many web systems try to understand a post, video, review, or conversation by looking at several kinds of evidence at once. A sentiment example may have spoken words, facial expression, and audio tone. A product or social post may have image, text, and behavior signals. In the clean classroom version, every example has every kind of evidence. In the real web version, pieces are often missing: a device may not capture one signal, a network transfer may fail, or a privacy setting may block a channel. This paper serves systems that still need to classify the content when only part of the evidence arrives. The main danger is not merely that less information is available. It is that the system may change the meaning of a class depending on which inputs are present. HiCoD tries to keep each category fixed in a shared meaning map, so a partial example is judged against the same class anchors as a complete example.
wh: The hard part is that different input types do not lose information in the same way. Text may preserve explicit words while losing tone. Audio may preserve emotion while losing the speaker's visual context. A fused complete example can define one center for a class, while an incomplete example can land somewhere else because the missing channel no longer helps pull it into place. The abstract calls this anchor drift: the class prototype, or the representative center of a category, shifts between complete and incomplete views. Once that happens, the model is no longer just uncertain; it is using a warped map. A sad utterance with missing video may be compared against a different idea of sadness than a sad utterance with all channels present. Prior reconstruction methods try to fill the missing channel, and alignment methods try to make channels agree, but the paper argues that both can still fail to preserve stable class geometry under partial inputs.
naive: A smart beginner might first train a model on complete examples, then, when a channel is missing, replace the missing piece with zeros, an average value, or a guessed reconstruction. Another simple plan is to train separate readers for text, audio, and video, then average their answers when only some are available. These ideas fail because they treat missing evidence as a local repair problem. The deeper problem is the shape of the class map. If the repaired or partial example is pulled away from the complete example's class center, the model may compare it to the wrong neighbors. The system can appear to align channels while still moving the category anchors, so generalization degrades when missingness patterns change.
ap: HiCoD's central move is to make the class anchors explicit and then train every version of an example to respect them. It builds a modality-aware semantic graph, meaning a relationship map that records how different input types and meanings should support one another when observations are partial. It also uses two levels of anchors. At the broad level, large-language-model-derived category descriptions provide global prototypes: stable reference points for what each class should mean. At the local level, top-K exemplars provide nearby concrete cases, preserving details that a broad category description might smooth away. The model then teaches, or distills, several internal views to agree inside one anchor space: single-channel features, fused multi-channel features, and prompt-completed signals. The goal is not to hallucinate the missing modality as perfectly real, but to keep the decision geometry stable when the input is incomplete.
mech: The input is a multimodal example, such as one from CMU-MOSI or CMU-MOSEI, where sentiment-related evidence may arrive through text, speech, and visual behavior, but some modalities may be absent. First, HiCoD treats the available modalities as partial observations rather than pretending the missing channel is harmless. It uses a modality-aware semantic graph to restore cross-modal structure: nodes can be understood as pieces of evidence or semantic units, and links say which pieces should inform one another across modalities. This lets information travel from observed channels toward the shared meaning structure without requiring every original signal to be present. Second, it builds class anchors at two scales. Global category prototypes come from a language model's category-level knowledge, giving broad semantic reference points. Local anchors come from the top-K exemplars, the nearby training cases most relevant to the current input, so the system keeps concrete modality-specific detail. Third, it aligns several representations into the same anchored space. A unimodal feature from one channel, a fused representation from several channels, and a prompt-completed signal are all trained to point toward compatible class anchors. The output is a classifier whose class geometry is meant to remain stable under fixed missing patterns and random missingness, reducing the shift between complete and incomplete views.
math: The main mathematical object is a shared representation space, a numeric map where examples and class anchors can be compared by nearness. This paper's problem forces that object because the model must compare incomplete and complete observations even though they contain different evidence. Similarity is the first idea: if a partial text-only example and a full text-audio-video example express the same class, the map should place them near the same class anchor. The danger is that closeness compresses many details into one distance, so HiCoD adds structure rather than relying on one flat comparison. The semantic graph is a network: evidence pieces are connected so information can move along meaningful cross-modal relations, while the method must avoid letting a missing or weak modality drag the whole map away. The anchors are prototypes, which are representative points for classes. Global prototypes express the broad category meaning, while local exemplars express nearby concrete cases. Distillation means training one set of signals to imitate the useful structure held by another; here, unimodal, fused, and prompt-completed signals are made consistent. The tradeoff is coherence versus detail: the model needs one stable class geometry, but it must not erase modality-specific clues that help distinguish close cases.
dots: This paper sits in the conference's broader multimodal family, where systems must make unlike evidence cooperate: words, images, audio, video, graphs, and user behavior. It connects most directly to similarity work because its central question is what should count as the same class when the observed channels differ. It also connects to graph reasoning because HiCoD uses a semantic graph to let evidence travel through relationships instead of treating each channel as isolated. It is near retrieval and recommendation papers that face sparse evidence: when a user, item, or document lacks one signal, the system must borrow structure from related examples without inventing false certainty. It also neighbors trust and safety multimodal papers, such as missing-modality meme or harmful-content detection, where absence of one channel can change the apparent meaning. The shared pressure is web incompleteness: real systems rarely receive the neat complete input assumed by simple training setups.
ww: HiCoD should improve over the naive approach because it attacks the source of the error: moving class centers. If a model only fills in missing inputs, the filled value can look plausible while still placing the example in the wrong region of the decision map. If it only aligns channels pairwise, each channel may agree locally while the overall class shape still shifts between complete and incomplete cases. Anchoring gives the model fixed reference points that do not depend solely on the currently observed channels. The global category prototype says, in effect, what the class should mean at a broad semantic level. The local top-K exemplars keep the anchor from becoming too abstract by tying it to nearby real cases. The semantic graph helps because missingness is not random noise in an empty room; modalities often carry related evidence. Text, audio, and visual cues can partly support one another. Multi-level distillation then makes consistency a repeated constraint across single-channel, fused, and prompt-completed views, so no one path is allowed to define a drifting class map by itself.
po: The payoff is a multimodal learner that remains useful when key evidence is absent. According to the abstract, HiCoD is tested on CMU-MOSI, CMU-MOSEI, and additional benchmarks, under both fixed missing patterns and random missingness. It reports stronger results than prior methods, including an Acc-2 gain of up to 6.4 points over MPLMM. In practical terms, the claimed capability is not just a better score. It is a way to classify web-scale multimodal content when devices, transmission failures, or privacy controls remove channels, while keeping the class meanings more stable between complete and incomplete inputs.
limits: The claim depends on the missing inputs still leaving enough related evidence for the graph and anchors to recover useful structure. If all channels that distinguish two classes are absent, stable anchors cannot create missing facts. The approach also assumes that language-model-derived global category prototypes are suitable reference points, and that the top-K local exemplars are genuinely relevant rather than misleading neighbors. The abstract reports benchmark gains, but it does not prove behavior across every web domain, every privacy pattern, or every kind of modality failure. It also does not show from the abstract alone how sensitive the method is to graph construction, exemplar selection, prompt quality, or categories whose meanings are culturally ambiguous.
